title: Ageing and digital services study
transcript:
[00:00:08] INT: Thanks again for sitting down with me today, Seamus. Just to confirm for the recording, you're happy to go ahead with the interview?
[00:00:15] P: Ah, I am, yeah. No bother at all. My full name is Seamus O'Sullivan, and I'm happy enough to have a chat if it helps somebody else down the line.
[00:00:26] INT: Brilliant, thank you. To start us off, could you tell me a little bit about yourself and your background here in County Cork?
[00:00:34] P: Well, I'm 70 years old now—born on the 14th of March, 1955, right here in Ballykieran. I lived my whole life by the water. For over forty years I worked out of the harbour with Ballykieran Marine Fisheries Co-op. Most folks around here just call it Ballykieran Marine, or BMFC on the paperwork. I started as a deckhand when I was seventeen and worked my way up. By the time I retired in June 2019, I skippered the only wooden-hulled scallop dredger left in Ballykieran. Fierce proud of that boat, I was.
[00:01:14] INT: That sounds like a remarkable career. It must have been a big adjustment when you retired.
[00:01:21] P: It was, and it wasn't, at first. My late wife, Bridget O'Sullivan, she was still with me then. We had a grand couple of years after I finished up with Padraig Foley—he was the fleet manager at Ballykieran Marine. Mr. Foley was a tough man to work for, mind you, always watching the clock and the fuel bills, though Foley had a decent heart underneath it all. Anyway, Bridget and I had plans to do a bit of travelling around the country. Then she got sick, and she passed away in November 2021. That's when the house got very quiet.
[00:02:02] INT: I'm very sorry to hear about Bridget. Do you still live in the same house?
[00:02:08] P: I do, yeah. 14 Harbour View Terrace, up in the Kilmore part of town. It's a grand little terrace, just a ten-minute walk down to the pier, though my legs aren't what they used to be. I have osteoarthritis in my left knee from years of standing on a wet deck in heavy swells. On damp mornings, getting down the stairs is a slow business.
[00:02:35] INT: Do you have family nearby who pop in?
[00:02:40] P: My daughter, Siobhan Gallagher, lives up in Dublin with her husband Declan and the two grandkids. Siobhan is great—she rings me every Sunday evening without fail, and she comes down to County Cork whenever she can get the time off work. But Dublin is a long drive, and they've their own busy lives. I don't like to be mithering her about every little thing.
[00:03:06] INT: And what about friends or neighbours around Kilmore?
[00:03:11] P: Most of the lads I fished with are either gone or not great on their feet either. My old crewmate, Tommy Cronin, he lives over the other side of Ballykieran. Tommy and I used to meet for a pint of a Friday, or walk down to the Cove Men's Shed on a Tuesday morning. He's had a rough winter with his chest, though, so we haven't been out as much. And you know yourself, the winter evenings are long when you're looking at four walls.
[00:03:43] INT: How do you usually spend your days now, Seamus?
[00:03:48] P: Well, I try to keep the hands busy. I have a little workshop out in the back shed, and my hobby is restoring vintage brass ship's compasses. I pick them up at car boot sales or old marine auctions, strip them down, polish the brass, balance the needles. It's fiddly work, especially before I had my cataract surgery last year, because my eyesight was getting hazy. Since the operation, though, I can see the fine screws again. It passes the afternoon.
[00:04:22] INT: That's a fascinating hobby. Have you ever thought about selling them or showing them online?
[00:04:29] P: Ah, God no. That's where I get completely lost. Siobhan bought me a tablet two Christmases ago so we could do the video calls, and she set up an email address for me—seamus.osullivan55@example.com. I can just about open an email if I have my reading glasses on, and I can press the green button when Siobhan rings on the video. Beyond that, the internet is a foreign country to me.
[00:05:00] INT: That brings us neatly to what we're looking at in this study—how older people experience digital services, especially for health, banking, and social care. Have you had to use online services much recently?
[00:05:14] P: Too much, if you ask me! Everything is pushing you onto a screen now. Take the banking. I've been with the West Cork Coastal Credit Union for thirty-five years. I used to walk in, hand my book across the counter, have a bit of a chat with the girls, and get my cash. Now they're always telling me to download the app. I get my state pension of 277 euros a week, and a small bit from the BMFC pension scheme, and I like to see it written down on paper. Last month I had to pay 1,450 euros for a new boiler, and trying to sort out the transfer online nearly gave me a heart attack.
[00:05:56] INT: What happened with the transfer?
[00:06:00] P: They wanted a code sent to my mobile phone—my number is 087 555 0142—and by the time I found my glasses and typed the six numbers into the tablet, the screen said the session had timed out. Three times that happened. In the end, I had to ring Siobhan in tears of frustration, and she talked me through it over the landline. It makes you feel foolish, you know? I spent forty years navigating trawlers in Force 8 gales, and I can't pay a plumber without my daughter holding my hand.
[00:06:35] INT: That's a really common frustration, Seamus. You're definitely not alone in feeling that way. What about government or social care services? Have you had to deal with any of those online?
[00:06:47] P: I have, yeah. When I applied for the fuel allowance and a bit of home help support after Bridget died, they told me to register on GovConnect Ireland. I had to dig out my social care reference number—SC-904821—and upload a photo of my passport. How am I supposed to take a clear photo of a passport on a tablet when my hands shake a bit in the morning? I gave up on it for two months.
[00:07:17] INT: How did you get it sorted in the end?
[00:07:21] P: It was Mrs. Eileen Barry, the community social care worker. She's an absolute saint. Eileen called out to 14 Harbour View Terrace on the 12th of January, sat at my kitchen table with a cup of tea, and did the whole thing with me on her laptop. She didn't make me feel stupid once. She just said the system wasn't built for people who didn't grow up with computers.
[00:07:47] INT: Having that face-to-face support sounds like it made a huge difference.
[00:07:52] P: Oh, night and day. And it's the same with the doctor. I go to Dr. Niamh Kavanagh over at Harbourside Medical Centre. I have mild atrial fibrillation, so I'm on blood thinners and I have to get my bloods checked regularly. A few months ago, Harbourside Medical Centre brought in an online booking system for repeat prescriptions and appointments. If you ring the reception, there's a recorded voice telling you to go to the website. Now, Dr. Kavanagh herself is brilliant—she told me to ignore the recording and just ask for the nurse if I'm stuck—but you still feel like you're being a nuisance.
[00:08:33] INT: Do you think the move to digital services affects how lonely or isolated you feel?
[00:08:40] P: Definitely. People don't realise that for someone living on their own, going into the post office, or the Credit Union, or the chemist, that might be the only real conversation you have all day. When you replace a person behind a desk with a website, you're taking away that bit of human contact. I pay 65 euros a month for broadband into the house just so I can keep up with these forms and talk to Siobhan, and half the time the connection drops anyway when the wind comes off the bay.
[00:09:14] INT: That's a significant chunk out of a weekly pension as well.
[00:09:19] P: It is, yeah. 65 euros a month is no small thing when you're heating an old house. Sometimes I wonder if I'd be better off cancelling it, but then I wouldn't see the grandkids on the screen, and I'd be completely cut off from GovConnect Ireland and the bank.
[00:09:38] INT: Have you ever tried any computer classes, maybe at the Cove Men's Shed or in Cork City?
[00:09:45] P: I went to one session at the library in Ballykieran last autumn. The young fella teaching it was very nice, but he went way too fast. He was talking about clouds and browsers and cookies, and I was sitting there thinking about biscuits! I didn't go back. If someone sat down one-to-one, like Eileen did, and showed me just the three things I actually need—how to check my bank, how to order my blood thinners from Dr. Kavanagh, and how to use the email—I'd learn it grand. I'm not thick, I just need it explained in plain English.
[00:10:22] INT: That makes complete sense. If you could tell the people designing these digital services one thing, what would it be?
[00:10:30] P: Keep a phone number with a real human being at the end of it. Don't assume everyone has a smartphone in their pocket or a daughter in Dublin to bail them out. Technology is grand when it works, and I'm grateful I can see Siobhan and Declan on a Sunday, don't get me wrong. But it shouldn't replace a friendly face.
[00:10:53] INT: That's a very clear message, Seamus. Thank you so much for your time and for being so open with me today.
[00:11:00] P: You're very welcome. Put the kettle on before you go, sure, there's no rush.

identifiers.text: skippered the only wooden-hulled scallop dredger left in Ballykieran
